title: How to Use Google Gemini to Brainstorm Content and Thought Leadership
content: In almost any organization, there are practically infinite content ideas hiding in memos, emails, presentation decks, and meeting notes. But too often, this material mostly sits idle. Ideas that sparked excitement in the moment get ignored in favor of the countless little emergencies of office life, and eventually they are forgotten entirely. Even with many companies actively encouraging their executives to post organic thought leadership on professional networking sites, social media, and company channels, there are countless missed opportunities to turn off-the-cuff insights into valuable content. Google Gemini can help you transform your meeting notes into content plans, on-brand slogan ideas, and even booth mock-ups for your events team. Step 1: Brainstorm Blog Ideas Imagine you’ve just stepped out of a meeting with your social media team leads. You have a document full of notes (or maybe even a transcript) about what resonates with your audience, trending topics in your industry, target audience data, and keywords that are effective at driving engagement with your brand. Instead of letting this wealth of information stay locked inside your notes, open up a new Gemini chat and brainstorm how to turn your team’s sprawling strategy session into a series of relevant, focused blog posts. Here’s a prompt you can try: Generate a list of four relevant and engaging thought leadership blog post ideas for [company] based on trending topics, target audience analysis, and brand keywords. Gemini will return ideas for blog posts with catchy, clickable titles, along with information about target audience, keywords, angle, and tone. For example, if your meeting notes talk about how your customers are worried about their employees using unauthorized IT tools, Gemini might suggest a blog post titled “The Anatomy of a Zombie Subscription: How to Audit and Kill Shadow IT Instantly.” Step 2: Develop the Material The initial output will just be kernels of potential blog posts, but you can go back and forth with Gemini to develop them into real content. Take the “Zombie Subscription” blog, for example. You might ask Gemini to give you options for a “four tips” article structure, or to identify specific ideas from your meeting notes that merit extra attention. Use your own judgment—and your own language—during this process, rather than having Gemini write your entire blog post for you. Gemini can help with brainstorming, outlining, drafting, and revision, but your audience is ultimately reading the content to hear your own expert insights. Step 3: Distill the Main Message Maybe during your meeting, your team also discussed launching a new brand campaign. You know that your customers value your reliable and unique services, and your company has a long history of delivering for its customers. But sometimes, it can feel impossible to condense these big ideas into a few words that really communicate why customers come back to your company over and over. If you need help getting started with ideas for a new campaign tagline, open a new chat in Gemini and prompt something like: Generate three options for a new slogan emphasizing reliability, innovation, and a long history of popularity for [company]. For a B2B fintech company, Gemini might offer options like “Innovating Beyond the Bank. Trusted with Billions.” Or: “Built for Tomorrow. Proven by $10 Billion Today.” You may not hit the mark exactly on your first prompt. Maybe you want more (or less) alliteration, for example. Maybe you want it to be five words or fewer, unbroken by punctuation. You can keep asking Gemini for new variations until the new tagline is just right. Step 4: Mock Up Visuals for Events Often, one successful creative project sparks ideas for another. After you create your blog campaign and craft your new slogan, you might turn your attention to upcoming events. Try mocking up booth graphics ideas for your events team. Here’s a sample prompt: Create an image of a trade show booth using orange and blue colors. The booth should be modern and showcase interactive computer stations. Gemini will generate an image that you can sketch on in-app, giving you a quick, no-risk way to play with your potential trade show setup. And between the blog posts, the tagline, and the event visuals, you will have turned a couple of pages of messy meeting notes into the bones of an entire marketing campaign.

title: What Anthropic Doomsayer Jacob Coxon Saw
content: Yesterday, Amir and I examined the shock waves that have rippled through the AI industry and far beyond since former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon very publicly quit his job over concerns that AI “could kill us all”—and another Anthropic AI safety specialist put the probability of such a catastrophe at greater than 10%. Coxon told me that is hardly the most pessimistic view inside Anthropic. “People have varying probabilities that—barring some substantial coordinated slowdown—the whole thing ends in doom,” he said in an interview later Wednesday. Those estimates range higher than 50% among some Anthropic employees, he said. Coxon was able to gauge the fears of his fellow employees because “Anthropic has a substantially more transparent internal culture than OpenAI,” where Coxon worked for years before joining Anthropic in May. Coxon, who focused on the earliest stages of training AI models at Anthropic, said he decided to leave the company because he was gradually “starting to viscerally feel the fear of where the tech's going to be like the next two years or even the next one year.”

title: SpaceX Overhauls Data Center Build-Out, Potentially Slowing Expansion
content: Elon Musk is famous for his “move fast” management philosophy, which he demonstrated most starkly when he built new data centers for his AI startup in record time two years ago. But a new team of rocket engineers Musk recently installed to run his data centers is taking a very different approach. SpaceX is changing how it builds the giant facilities that house AI servers in a way that might slow the building of new campuses, according to people familiar with the situation. The new management team is looking to install more backup systems for power and cooling, and to more thoroughly test those systems before the data centers start operating, instead of adding them later on, as the AI company was doing, two of the people said. SpaceX also wants to reduce the use of temporary power and cooling systems in its data centers, one person said . In some cases, the new management is redesigning portions of existing data centers, the people said. The new approach marks a shift from the one xAI—Musk’s AI company, now part of SpaceX—took when it initially began building its giant Tennessee data center campus, Colossus, in 2024. At the time, Musk chose to prioritize speed and computing capacity over building out the infrastructure needed to increase reliability, the people said. But in late June, Musk shook up the management of SpaceX’s data center team, replacing data center veterans with people from SpaceX’s rocket launch team. (SpaceX acquired Musk’s xAI startup earlier this year.) The new management of the data center team told some staff when they took over this summer that SpaceX engineers had been brought in to improve reliability at the company’s facilities in Tennessee and Mississippi, two people said. Early on, frequent outages forced the company’s AI researchers to put projects on hold for hours at a time and lose some training progress, one person said. Reliability may be even more important for SpaceX now that it is renting out computing capacity to other companies, such as Anthropic and Google. Reliability had improved earlier this year but there are signs the management overhaul could be causing new problems. Construction work affected a power line and caused a high-profile outage at one of SpaceX’s massive data centers in Memphis, Tenn. last week, according to a person familiar with the situation. The outage knocked some of SpaceXAI’s Grok models offline and had ripple effects also hurting some of its compute customers, SpaceX said. A spokesperson for SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. Slower Build-Out Musk appears to support the new policy. In recent months, he has visited the facilities in Memphis on a nearly weekly basis, stopping by most Sundays, two people said. He most recently visited the site this past Sunday, they said. In the past, he repeatedly touted his company’s ability to rapidly build data centers as a key advantage in the AI race. SpaceX, which acquired Musk’s xAI startup earlier this year, even cited the speed factor in its initial public offering paperwork in June. SpaceX has said the AI unit brought its first data center online with 100,000 graphics processing units in just 122 days—an unprecedented timeline in the industry, where it can take years to build a data center of that size. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has praised the team’s efforts as “superhuman” and “unbelievable.” To move quickly, xAI brought on thousands of contractors and built different parts of the facility in parallel, with crews installing cooling pipes, pulling electrical and networking cable, and carrying out other work simultaneously, often in the same areas of the facility, rather than waiting for completion of one task before starting the next phase, the people said. But the speed has come with some trade-offs. Many big cloud firms set up their data centers in phases to ensure things go smoothly and the center can operate reliably, one person said. SpaceXAI’s process included bringing the minimum power and cooling infrastructure for the data center online before finishing backup systems, and then adding some of those backups months later, people familiar with the matter said. The company has relied on temporary power and cooling systems, such as dozens of gas turbines, since the data centers opened, one person said. When they first came online, the company’s first two data centers had only a fraction of the redundancy of data centers other hyperscalers operated, the person familiar with the design said. That left them vulnerable to outages, because a single equipment failure could take entire clusters offline, the person said. Individuals on the data center team also had the authority to approve changes to construction plans and equipment, and they could buy equipment as needed rather than optimizing for costs, the people said. At times, that meant that there was a mix of different parts used in the data centers, rather than a uniform supply of racks and servers, one person said. That could also undermine reliability, another person familiar with the situation said. To be sure, while building backup systems earlier and doing more testing is likely to slow the construction process, SpaceX probably won’t abandon xAI’s accelerated construction model entirely, one person said. Data Center Exodus SpaceX completed its acquisition of xAI in February, at a time when the startup was heavily burning cash. A few months after the deal closed, SpaceX leaders held information-gathering meetings with members of the data center team, one of the people said. (SpaceX held similar meetings at xAI’s office in Palo Alto, Calif., shortly before dozens of engineers left the startup.) Over the past few weeks, more than a dozen leaders on the data center project have left the team, replaced with SpaceX engineers and leaders with manufacturing and operations backgrounds outside data center construction. The exits came shortly after SpaceX’s Wesley Salandro took over leadership of the team from Dan Rowland, who had led the infrastructure engineering and at one point had reported directly to Musk. Salandro has worked at SpaceX for more than seven years and was vice president of production for the Falcon and Dragon rockets. Rowland, a leader on Tesla’s Dojo supercomputer project before he joined xAI in 2024, left shortly after Salandro took over. Along with Salandro, SpaceX leadership issued a call for some of its rocket and Starlink engineers in Bastrop, Texas and Cape Canaveral, Florida to volunteer to help with the data centers for six to eight week rotations, two people said. More than 1,300 engineers volunteered and over 300 SpaceX engineers have joined the data center project over the past month, they said. Within a few weeks, Jake Palmer, who led physical infrastructure for SpaceXAI, left. So did Logan Beach, head of security for data centers; Tiffany Wilson, head of procurement for data centers; and Pablo Mendoza, head of data center finance. Aakash Verma, SpaceXAI’s project engineer for its Duke Energy site also left to join OpenAI in August, along with Brent Mayo, who was the manager of site builds at SpaceXAI. Liz Balke, who helped design the data centers, now works on the infrastructure team at Anthropic. SpaceX leaders have also added more middle managers in recent months to what was once a relatively flat organizational structure, two people said. This means workers have less autonomy to approve equipment orders or make decisions onsite which can slow down the build process, the people said. There could be more shake-ups to come. After last week’s data center outage, Musk wrote on X that the company was “taking corrective action to ensure this does not happen again.”

title: Jeffrey Katzenberg Teams Up with Former OpenAI Sora Head on New AI Video Startup
content: Hollywood mogul Jeffrey Katzenberg is teaming up with the former head of OpenAI’s Sora app to launch a new AI startup that would train its own video models and try to win over filmmakers, people familiar with the matter said. The founders have been talking to potential investors including Andreessen Horowitz about raising significant funding for the new company, the people said. Bill Peebles, the former OpenAI video researcher, would start the company with Katzenberg, former co-founder of DreamWorks and CEO of DreamWorks Animation, and Sujay Jaswa, former CFO of Dropbox. Katzenberg and Jaswa now run Wndr, a tech investment firm that also incubates companies. The new company, whose name couldn’t be learned, would be Katzenberg’s most ambitious venture since Quibi, a short-form video app that raised $1.75 billion before folding in 2020. The company would develop new video models as some major AI companies like OpenAI pull back on AI for video initiatives in the U.S. while Chinese firms like ByteDance plow ahead but face significant copyright problems. OpenAI shut down Sora , which briefly hit No. 1 on Apple’s app store, earlier this year due to its high costs and computing needs and the company’s desire to focus on other business-related products. Peebles left the company soon after. Among other AI giants, Google and Meta Platforms have announced new video models this year. And AI startups in the U.S. have raised hundreds of millions of dollars in funding to build video-generating AI models. These include Runway, last valued at $5.3 billion, and Higgsfield, last valued at $5.4 billion. Higgsfield focuses more on individual creators and businesses, though, and largely sells access to third party models, including Seedance, though it also offers its own family of AI video models called Soul. Runway does work with some Hollywood studios including Paramount and Lionsgate, but it also sells its models to ad agencies, retail brands and individual creators. ByteDance’s Seedance model, meanwhile, has recently touted major improvements in its video-generating capabilities. However, the company put its release on pause in March due to a string of copyright disputes with major Hollywood studios and streaming platforms before eventually releasing it globally to countries excluding the U.S. Wndr, launched in 2016, has invested in dozens of companies including Databricks and Waymo, and has helped build startups in fields ranging from cybersecurity to longevity. Katzenberg’s creative credentials—before launching DreamWorks with Steven Spielberg and David Geffen, he headed Walt Disney Studios—could help the new company gain traction with an entertainment industry that has been ambivalent about AI. Some studio executives and filmmakers have embraced the idea of AI-generated video—Walt Disney Co. had an investment and licensing deal with OpenAI before Sora’s demise. But others have raised serious concerns that AI could inhibit creativity, displace talent and steamroll intellectual property protections.

title: BAM identifies lithium isotopes as diagnostic tool for battery ageing - electrive.com
content:
Researchers at the Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing have discovered that the distribution of two lithium isotopes in the cells is directly linked to degradation processes, like a fingerprint. This insight is intended to help better understand the ageing mechanisms of batteries.
Symbolic image: A typical high-voltage battery for electric cars.
Image: Stellantis
The service life of lithium-ion batteries is limited by complex ageing processes, the causes of which are often difficult to distinguish. Researchers at BAM have demonstrated that examining the lithium isotopes within the cells can provide valuable insights, as they explain in an article published in the journal
ACS Energy Letters
Specifically, the team led by Carlos Abad and Beatrice Battistella used the distribution of two lithium isotopes within a cell as a diagnostic tool for ageing processes. The key finding: “Their characteristic traces and patterns provide a fingerprint of the underlying degradation mechanisms,” states a BAM press release.
The background is that multiple complex processes inside the battery contribute to degradation. “To date, the challenge of clearly identifying these aging mechanisms and distinguishing them from one another remains unresolved. While conventional diagnostic methods show that a battery is aging, they often provide only limited information about when, where, and by what mechanism degradation is triggered,” the Federal Institute for Materials Research and Testing (BAM) explained.
The newly developed method leverages the fact that natural lithium consists of two isotopes: lithium-6 and the slightly heavier lithium-7. These are variants of the same chemical element with a different number of neutrons, as the research team explains. In new batteries, both lithium isotopes are distributed in the same ratio as in all natural occurrences of the alkali metal, i.e., 2.4 per cent to 97.6 per cent.
The researchers specifically examined a lithium battery with a cathode made of lithium-nickel-manganese-cobalt oxide and a graphite anode. According to the scientists, lithium-6 began to accumulate preferentially at the anode after just the first few charge cycles. After a further 280 cycles, this effect intensified, while the cathode exhibited a significantly increased lithium-7 content. At the same time, the cells’ capacity decreased.
According to BAM, the detection was made possible by a high-resolution form of mass spectrometry, which allowed the distribution of lithium isotopes to be determined layer by layer across the entire depth of the electrodes. The investigations were carried out in collaboration with Nu Instruments Ltd. in the UK and the Leibniz Institute for Solid State and Materials Research Dresden (IFW Dresden).
“The distribution of lithium isotopes thus provides direct information about aging processes in lithium-ion batteries. The isotopes act as natural markers. Their distribution provides insight into the mechanisms that controls lithium movement during battery operation and where changes occur,” said Beatrice Battistella. The researchers were also able to demonstrate that these traces are closely linked to the batteries’ capacity loss.
For BAM, the significance of the results lies primarily in their potential applications for precise measurements: instead of detecting ageing solely through capacity loss, it could in the future be tracked much earlier based on the traces left by lithium isotopes in the battery cell. “This enables a more precise understanding of aging mechanisms and is ultimately crucial for improving batteries in a more targeted manner and predicting their service life more accurately,” concludes the institute.

title: Battery storage startup Rebaba secures nearly €4 million - electrive.com
content:
Rebaba, a startup from Sweden founded by former Northvolt employees, has raised just under €4 million euros in a seed funding round. The company plans to use the funds to expand its business with second-life battery storage systems.
Rebaba founders Paula Runsten and Felix Kruse
Image: Rebaba
Founded in Stockholm in 2023, Rebaba focuses on the concept of a second life. Similar to German battery storage startup
Voltfang
, decommissioned EV batteries are given a second life in stationary energy storage systems. Rebaba refers to these as circular battery storage systems.
Rebaba has now raised 44.1 million SEK in an oversubscribed seed funding round led by Sistafund and EIT Urban Mobility, with participation from existing shareholders and new European investors. This amount is equivalent to nearly 4 million euros.
Advancing circular battery storage systems
This capital injection will enable Rebaba to advance its mission of delivering circular battery storage systems that address the challenges of climate change as well as globally growing demand for stable and cost-effective energy on a large scale. By combining reclaimed EV batteries with its patent-pending Rebaba technology, the company aims to help its customers reduce energy costs, avoid grid congestion, increase operational reliability, generate revenue from green energy, and simultaneously build a circular economy for batteries.
Rebaba currently offers two energy storage products: Companion, a compact, cabinet-based 40-kWh system for private and small commercial applications, and Containerised, a larger-scale system for commercial and industrial applications. The latter enables customers to implement load shifting, local generation storage, peak shaving, and grid balancing services.
Rebaba plans to increase the capacity of its CircularHub production facility in Stockholm to 40 MWh per year, which could avoid approximately 4,000 tonnes of CO₂ annually. Additionally, the company intends to open further production sites in Europe. For the distribution of its battery storage systems in Europe, Rebaba has already entered into partnerships with various companies, including a
collaboration with Cologne-based startup Nanuq
(link in German).
Paula Runsten, co-founder and CEO of Rebaba, explains: “Demand for energy storage is accelerating globally, driven by AI, electrification, and the transition to renewables. Conventional thinking is that we must produce new batteries for every energy storage system being deployed, but this simply isn’t true. Electric vehicle batteries are retired with 70-80% of their useful life remaining, and by 2028, returning EV batteries are projected to offer more usable capacity annually than the entire global demand for stationary battery storage. The batteries already exist. Our job is to make reuse scalable.”
Marie Geneste, Partner at investor Sistafund, adds: “Europe’s energy transition depends on scaling storage fast, without creating new dependencies on scarce raw materials or costly imports. Rebaba turns retired EV batteries into high-performance storage systems that can be built locally and compete on price. That is what convinced us to lead this round: circularity without compromise, and a team with the potential to build a European leader in energy storage.”

title: Fraunhofer ISE increases energy density of battery cells - electrive.com
content:
The Fraunhofer ISE has developed a new architecture for battery cells that is said to enable 10 to 15 per cent higher energy density at the same weight. The approach uses significantly thicker electrodes, which reduces the need for current collectors. This could also potentially be of interest for electric vehicles.
Semi-automated production of battery cells at Fraunhofer ISE
Image: Fraunhofer ISE
Developing battery cells with higher energy density while maintaining the same weight enables more energy to be stored in the same space. This offers advantages for stationary battery storage systems, which were the focus of three research projects funded by the German Federal Government at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE in Freiburg. The physical insights gained can also be applied to traction batteries for electric vehicles, where higher energy density could extend vehicle range.
In the projects at Fraunhofer ISE, the institute collaborated with various partners to develop a new architecture for battery cells that achieves higher energy density. The researchers focused on the electrodes, increasing their coating thickness by more than threefold: instead of the previously typical 100 to 200 micrometres, they applied coatings of up to 800 micrometres.
Battery cells with 10 to 15 per cent higher energy density
According to the research institution, this has increased the energy density of the cells by 10 to 15 percent, depending on the battery type and design. The reasoning is that, in a battery cell, electrode coatings and current collectors alternate in many thin layers. The coating contains the active material that stores energy, while the current collectors conduct the electrical current. By making the electrodes thicker, fewer of these layers – and thus fewer current collectors – are needed. This leaves more space for active material at the same cell weight.
“Normally, the anode and cathode – the two electrodes of a battery cell -consist of many thin, alternating layers of electrode coating and current collectors,” explains Dr. Oliver Fitz, Group Leader for Battery Cell Technology at Fraunhofer ISE. “We’ve managed to increase the thickness of the electrode coating from the previously standard 100 to 200 micrometers to up to 800 micrometers, thereby significantly reducing the number of current collectors required. As a result, we have much more space for active material, which increases the energy density by 10 to 15 percent, depending on the battery type and design.”
Focus on battery storage system applications
However, the concept is not yet ready for series production. According to Fraunhofer ISE, the project results instead demonstrate a “promising approach toward the future industrialization of this novel electrode and cell architecture”. The new battery cells are particularly interesting for use in battery energy storage systems (BESS), but also in electric vehicles.
The research team developed the new electrode and cell design as part of the projects “VORAN – Innovative Sodium-Ion Battery Storage for Stationary and Mobile Applications” (running until June 2027), “INFAB – Zinc-Ion Batteries for Stationary Energy Storage – Manufacturing and Assembly” (completed), and “WinZIB2 – Globally Deployable, Innovative Zinc-Ion Battery System”, all of which were funded by the German Federal Government.

title: Results of Donut Lab's Nail Penetration Safety Test
content:

Explore Donut Lab's solid-state battery claims, nail penetration test results, and insights into their solid-state pouch cell technology.
September 9, 2026
7 Slides
Start slideshow
Donut Lab's customer base is diverse and ranges from vehicles to drones and battery energy storage systems.
Donut Lab
Donut Lab has been making waves in the battery industry with bold claims of unprecedented performance metrics, including 400 Wh/kg energy density, 100,000-cycle life, and five-minute charging capabilities. These claims, unveiled at CES 2026, have drawn both
excitement and skepticism
, placing the Finnish startup under intense scrutiny. But without independent validation, critical questions remained unanswered.
In this context, Donut Lab announced the results of new tests, including a nail penetration test on its so-called solid-state pouch cell, which assesses the battery's safety and structural integrity under extreme conditions. The test offers a rare glimpse into the real-world performance of a promising technology. As the industry struggles with the need for standardized testing and third-party validation, this independent assessment is a crucial step toward bridging the credibility gap for any new technology.
Related:
Organic Flow Batteries Meet Steel Tank Infrastructure for Grid-Scale Energy Storage
Donut Lab announced that VTT, an independent research organization, found the company’s battery achieved an energy density of 409 watt-hours per kilogram and 805 watt-hours per liter. “This was a fairly straightforward test, as energy density consists of two things: how much energy a battery cell holds and how much it weighs or takes up space," says Ville Piippo, CTO at Donut Lab.
However, Donut Lab did not specify the type or chemistry of the battery cells during the nail penetration testing. In the test report, Intertek selected the option "not given by the manufacturer" in the battery type/chemistry section, leaving the cells' exact composition undisclosed. The nail penetration test was conducted on a solid-state pouch cell, as described in the report under the test samples section, but it does not reference the cell's structural design.
With Donut Lab's claims under the spotlight and the broader solid-state battery landscape evolving rapidly, this test's results could offer valuable insight into the viability of their technology. However, it may be too late for Donut Lab to rebuild public trust. Explore the slideshow to gain detailed insights and visual highlights of the test results.

title: How Orchestration is Redefining Supply Chain Strategy
content:
How Orchestration is Redefining Supply Chain Strategy
Prioritise Us
on Google
Ashley Naughton and Margaret Ngari discuss how supply chain leaders can move from siloed functions to true orchestration at Supply Chain LIVE
Ashley Naughton and Margaret Ngari discuss how supply chain leaders can move from siloed functions to true orchestration at Supply Chain LIVE
Supply Chain LIVE
hosted its Supply Chain Orchestration Panel on September 9 examining how companies are using people, process and technology to bring visibility and resilience to its operations.
Taking on that topic were Ashley Naughton, Partner for Manufacturing Operations Improvement at PA Consulting and Margaret Ngari, Regional Supply Chain Director - East Africa joining as an Independent speaker.
Ashley brings a background across Rolls-Royce and automotive before moving into advisory, while Margaret has experience across financial services, government, FMCG, manufacturing and NGO supply chains from her base in Nairobi.
Defining orchestration
Rising supply chain complexity has driven a wave of new solutions promising greater efficiency and cost savings.
Supply chain orchestration
is built on coordinating and automating end-to-end processes, reducing the fragmentation and error that comes from disconnected systems and teams working in isolation.
"Orchestration means many, many different things and that's the problem," Ashley says. "I look at orchestration as a way to describe collaboration, the outcomes that a connected supply chain can deliver is much more powerful and meaningful than any single person or entity doing things on their own."
Not every solution fits every problem and some can create more disruption than they solve, relying on a cohesive effort.
"You have different people playing different instruments, but they have to sync in terms of producing good music," Margaret says. "If someone is off key, then it wouldn't be good."
The Supply Chain Orchestration Panel: Key Takeaways
Orchestration is misunderstood - the term means different things to different people, often causing confusion rather than clarity.
Technology comes second - real transformation starts with fixing processes and people, not buying new tools.
Culture decides adoption - even strong technology fails if teams and workplace culture don't accept it.
End-to-end mapping is a myth - supply chains shift too fast for full visibility to ever be fully achieved.
Risk management is the future skill - supply chain roles are evolving to require dedicated risk expertise, not just operational knowledge.
People before technology
Amid growing geopolitical and market volatility, real-time data has become one of the clearest ways for
supply chain leaders
to anticipate disruption rather than simply respond to it.
Full visibility into operations allows leaders to see exactly where support is needed before committing to a technology investment.
Margaret says: "Technology is really coming in, in terms of giving that data, checking the previous data and giving us predictions."
Businesses are automating more of their operations than ever, yet many still fail to see the results they expect.
The technology itself may not be flawed but it can be unsuccessful if not fully supported by human workers.
"There is a tendency more often than not to lean into technology to begin with," Ashley explains. "You start with the processes and the people and the technology actually is the latter part of the solution."
Even the most capable systems depend on the people expected to use them and without buy-in across teams, adoption stalls regardless of how well a solution is built.
Margaret says: "Technology cannot fully change what people do because there's that human element that needs to be brought in. If the team and the culture does not accept it then it's going to be hard for them to implement it."
Margaret Ngari, Regional Supply Chain Director - East Africa joining as an Independent speaker
Chasing end-to-end mapping
As supply chain complexity continues to rise, tracking every link across sprawling, ever-shifting supplier networks has become an increasingly resource-intensive and, for many organisations, unrealistic goal.
"Connected end-to-end supply chain, it's almost a myth. It will never occur," Ashley says. "Your supply chain changes more quickly than you can ever monitor and map it."
Rather than pursuing total visibility, orchestration relies on
automated coordination
directed at the areas of greatest risk, allowing technology to manage complexity that manual oversight alone cannot.
Ashley explains: "You need to decide what your segmentation strategy looks like and go after certain suppliers and allow technology to do the rest.
"Then you've got a fighting chance of how you manage that massive risk."
Data alone doesn't guarantee better decisions, and without the ability to interpret it correctly, increased visibility can generate noise rather than clarity.
"You need to have intelligence to interpret the data," Margaret says. "If we don't know what to do with it, then it ends up as a thousand notifications with no real action."
Orchestration means many, many different things and that's the problem.
Ashley Naughton, Partner for Manufacturing Operations Improvement at PA Consulting
Ashley Naughton, Partner for Manufacturing Operations Improvement at PA Consulting
Looking to the future
As agentic AI and digitalisation reshape how supply chains operate, orchestration is increasingly viewed as essential for navigating geopolitical and market volatility.
"Our supply chain roles will become much more complex," Ashley says. "It's going to be much more interconnected. It's going to be curated through intelligence, so you have to collaborate with your key suppliers, but you also have to use intelligence."
As automation takes on more of the operational load, the ability to manage risk is emerging as a distinct skill set in its own right, rather than a secondary responsibility layered onto existing roles.
"One of the greatest items that supply chain people will have, and which now is not there, is being risk managers," Margaret says. "We'll still need the people elements like agility, simplicity and risk managers."

title: The Big Rebrand: Supply Chains as a Strategic Growth Engine
content:
The Big Rebrand: Supply Chains as a Strategic Growth Engine
Prioritise Us
on Google
Kim Faulkner, Chief Supply Chain Officer at Tate & Lyle, led the opening keynote at Supply Chain LIVE
Kim Faulkner, Chief Supply Chain Officer at Tate & Lyle conducted the opening keynote speech at Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit
Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit kicked off on September 8 2026, with an opening keynote speech from Tate & Lyle's Chief Supply Chain Officer,
Kim Faulkner
Throughout the event, leaders from around the world took to the Supply Chain Stage and the workshops around the venue in order to share insights on the current challenges and solutions shaping the modern supply chain.
In her keynote,
The Big Rebrand: Supply Chain - The Strategic Growth Engine
, Kim explored how the role of the supply chain has changed in recent years, detailing how businesses are reacting to this shift.
The rebrand
In recent years, the supply chain has come out of the shadows somewhat, entering the boardroom as businesses recognise the critical role the function plays in operational success. With this, there has been a rebrand of the function – no longer is it all about efficiency and cost savings, but rather resilience and growth.
Tate & Lyle understands the idea of a rebrand very well, once being known as a sugar company. Now, the organisation is a specialty food and beverage organisation, working to reduce sugar, fat and calories in its products. Having sold its sugar business in 2010, the brand now works to make a whole host of foods healthier, including crackers, breakfast cereals and yogurts.
"None of that is possible without our amazing supply chain team at Tate & Lyle," Kim explained. "We take
scientific innovations
, manufacture and supply those to customers around the world that are helping to improve the health and nutrition of consumers."
For years, supply chains have been associated with efficiency within manufacturing sites, reduction of inventory and cost savings. However, that is changing. Kim states, "I believe in the future the supply chain will be known by something far greater, what we enable. Better customer experiences, faster and better decisions, more confident investments, higher profitable growth and a new generation of leaders who understand the whole business."
Tate & Lyle sold its sugar business and now prioritises making food and drinks healthier. Credit: Tate & Lyle
The catalyst
Many supply chain leaders have pointed to COVID-19 as a catalyst of this change. For them, it really brought the supply chain into the limelight, as everything came to a halt. Businesses could no longer operate as they were, with non-essential work being put on hold,
manufacturing
of PPE increasing and healthcare supply chains being under stress.
Since then, supply chain leaders have been brought into the boardroom, with their decisions being recognised as business and commercial decisions. During the pandemic, Kim was working for Colgate-Palmolive, making decisions on hand soap, based on what the suppliers for caps and labels could provide. That demonstrated how new strategies could be formed.
This has helped Kim navigate the turbulence supply chains are facing every day. As volatility and disruption become more common, resilience has entered the forefront of supply chain strategy.
Resilience
, a word that we will probably hear a hundred times this week is part of that contribution, but I believe resilience is misunderstood," she explains.
"It's not about avoiding every disruption. That is neither practical nor affordable. It's about identifying the signals earlier. It's about understanding the right trade-offs that we need to make, and it's about giving our businesses the confidence to grow in an uncertain world."
Kim Faulkner, Chief Supply Chain Officer at Tate & Lyle
The result
Supply chains have now been recognised as a strategic engine of growth. As a result, leaders need to understand how the supply chain can deliver on customer impact profit and revenue. Leaders now understand that the supply chain can unlock value, but still lack clarity as to how, and how much.
"In supply chains, we create tremendous value every day, but we don't always articulate it in the way that helps influence
business and commercial
decisions. Our story cannot end in operational metrics, but rather what those metrics make possible," Kim affirms.
"What does the big supply chain brand look like? It means we need to articulate our contribution beyond planning, making, sourcing and delivering. We need to build resilience before disruption strikes, allowing the business to grow with confidence. We need to speak the language of business, and we need to look at our operational priorities and accomplishments in the impact they have on customers and our commercial teams.
"We need to build strong relationships across our functions in the organisation and within our supply networks. We already have the invitation to contribute at a higher level. We earned that credibility during disruption. It's now our opportunity to turn that credibility into longer lasting influence."

title: Discussing Global Trade and Logistics at Supply Chain LIVE
content:
Discussing Global Trade and Logistics at Supply Chain LIVE
Prioritise Us
on Google
Leaders offered insights on global trade and logistics at Supply Chain LIVE
Leaders gathered at Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit to discuss the biggest challenges determining the current state of global trade and logistics
Uncertainty has become a defining feature of global trend in recent years, with the COVID-19 pandemic acting as a catalyst for ongoing disruption.
Now, supply chains around the world are re-making their strategies in order to navigate tariff policies, climate events, materials shortages, inflation and hostility.
At Supply Chain LIVE: The London Summit, leaders gathered to discuss the current trends shaping the industry, and the strategies that are helping leaders develop resilience.
Dennis Schmitz
, Managing Director UK at Arvato, and Margaret Ngari, Regional Supply Chain Director - East Africa, joined the event on the Global Trade and Logistics panel, where they explored strategies for optimising international supply chains.
Navigating complexity
Global trade has seen some significant shifts in recent years. The rise in ecommerce demand has increased cross-border B2C shipping, driven by social media trends and a rise in affordable platforms. In the B2B world, ongoing
volatility
has changed how businesses operate, as many organisations are moving towards supplier diversification.
Trade tensions and extreme climate events have contributed to a growth in sourcing – rather than relying on one supplier, businesses are creating supply chain relationships with suppliers from around the world. This helps mitigate the risk of regional disruption – if a supplier in one region is affected by a weather event, or trade regulations, the other suppliers can still contribute towards stock.
Not all businesses have operated this way, however, as some have moved towards a localised approach, bringing their suppliers closer to home so they can be in the same regulation zone or
climate bubble
. Different supply chains have moved in opposing ways, and both options have demonstrated strong results. However, this can add more complexity to an already strained supply chain ecosystem.
In recent years, Margaret has noticed a shift within the SME and NGO sector, supporting them throughout their growth as organisations recognise them and their importance to the wider supply chain. Alongside this, the supply chain itself has become a more recognised driver of success.
"Supply chain is no longer sitting in the backseat, but they've been brought to the table in boardrooms because we need to look at business continuity and strategic decisions," she explains.
Margaret Ngari, Regional Supply Chain Director - East Africa
"These are huge changes and we need to look at what are our risks, what are we holding back, what do we need to change? And not just saying that it's normal, what we plan at the beginning of the year should be the same end to end, but we've seen increasingly with the changes in geopolitical risks and also in tariffs, in policies, it's an ever-continuing process."
Meeting consumer demand
Global trade has so many more cogs in the machine than ever before, with a network of moving parts made up of suppliers, transportation providers, warehouse staff, manufacturers and more. With an increase in cross-border trade, there is also the matter of complex legislation and differing border requirements.
As technology has become more advanced and supply chains have become more complex, consumer and client expectations have grown. Now, they are expecting faster responses, increased delivery options and greater visibility into their operations.
"Complexity has significantly increased over the last couple of years, while at the same time client expectations haven't changed at all. If anything, they have increased," explains Dennis.
Dennis Schmitz, Managing Director UK at Arvato
"Nowadays with omnichannel, every end consumer expects their pass to be delivered essentially instantly across every single channel. So obviously navigating that puts lots of pressure on our clients and that is something that we try to navigate with them as best as possible."
Two businesses can offer the same products, but a sophisticated supply chain can act as the competitive advantage needed. Having strong visibility, inventory management and good transparency can cast the deciding vote for the consumer. Technology helps drive this, as it can offer real-time insights into stock levels and into a products' journey.
Having transparency creates more compliance, but it also helps inform the client more – are the costs of cross-border legislation something they can justify, can they meet the ideal levels of service? In today's world, transparency is critical for every cog in the global supply chain, from the supplier to the end consumer.
Flexibility in the supply chain
As the market changes so quickly, the most successful strategies are not the most solid ones. Instead, they are the ones that can move as demands move.
"When we're building global strategies in terms of logistics, we look at recent changes. Five, ten years ago, you'd create a strategy and it would run for two years, because there was no significant changes, explains Margaret.
"Now, there needs to be more adaptable strategies and not fixated that this is the strategy we are using . They need to be agile and adaptable to any changes and just not looking at tariffs, but looking at also what else can affect our strategy."
Having accurate data is a massive driver of remaining agile, as organisations can have an entire picture of their supply chains. At Arvato, Dennis and his team are seeing the benefits from
automation and AI
– tools which are helping collect more data, validate the data and drive transparency across the operation.
This allows for adaptability, which allows businesses to seize new opportunities – ones which were previously beyond their reach. Throughout the panel, Dennis and Margaret emphasised that transparency, flexibility and resilience are the key to withstanding the ongoing volatility in
global trade and logistics

title: Supply Chain LIVE: How are Leaders Developing Resilience?
content:
Supply Chain LIVE: How are Leaders Developing Resilience?
Prioritise Us
on Google
The Risk and Resilience panel discussed how manufacturers are moving away from reacting to supplier problems to build genuine visibility into their supply networks.
At Supply Chain LIVE, leaders from osapiens, Babcock International and Bugatti Rimac explore the importance of risk management and resilience
The world is facing more volatility than ever before, meaning businesses are more exposed to risk. In a year defined by tariffs, extreme climate events and conflict, businesses need to develop resilience strategies throughout their supply chain.
Now more than ever, discussions on these topics are critical.
Supply Chain LIVE
brought together a range of leaders from around the world, sharing insights on challenges, solutions and tools.
In a dedicated panel, leaders from the manufacturing industry explored how supply chains have changed in recent years and what they have been doing to minimise the impact of ongoing risk.
Will Fox, Senior Account Executive at osapiens, Ewan Sime, Global Director of Procurement and Supply Chain at Babcock International Group and Aurelien Faucheux, Procurement and Supply Chain Director and CPO at Bugatti Rimac discussed how their supply chains have changed in recent years, on a dedicated
Risk and Resilience panel
Changing risk
Founded in 2018 by a team with a background in track-and-trace technology, osapiens has grown to serve more than 2,500 customers with more than one million suppliers mapped through its systems. This vast network adds enough complexity, but new regulations and differing reporting requirements have introduced even more chaos to the supply chain role.
"All of that data already sits within your systems or within your suppliers.
osapiens
has created a hub for that sectioning, reporting into one section, product compliance into another, and then sustainability and risk supply risk management into other sections," explains Will.
Will Fox, Senior Account Executive, osapiens
"What you're getting is a full 360 degree view of all of your compliance requirements, your reporting requirements, as well as your tier end supplying by our mapping features."
In the past, risks were less interlinked. Quality issues, logistics issues or regional inflation issues were common, but they were more easily managed, or only hit one sector. Now, ongoing geopolitical risks are creating ripple effects, leading to interconnected risks around the world. Due to this, risks are much more complex and harder to tackle.
Reducing fragmentation
Amid increasing complexity, visibility throughout the supply chain is key. When supply chains have extensive partnerships, there needs to be clarity throughout, and open communication across each department to reduce the risk of fragmentation.
"More and more, transparency is key and getting some partners on board with us on the long term essential for our business. When you talk about visibility, it goes both ways," explains Aurelien.
Aurelien Faucheux, Procurement and Supply Chain Director and CPO at Bugatti Rimac
"So we need to explain what's going on in the market to our colleagues, to our CEO, to our CFO, explaining our actions and the potential impact. It is also important for us to explain what's going on in the market because we're not and they are not all buyers. We know what the market constraints are, but they don't know. So we have also to explain  what's going on in the market, what are the risks that we are facing as a company in order to make the right business decisions."
Single issues can have a major impact on supply chain workflows, but ensuring visibility across the tiers can help mitigate this risk. By having these insights, challenges can be spotted much earlier, meaning they can be taken care of before they impact a wider flow, or stopped before the event itself takes place. Moreover, increased visibility leads to more trust, which creates stronger relationships between partners, buyers and suppliers.
Rethinking strategy
For Babcock, building resilience has come through different methods of sourcing. Collaboration with SMEs has been crucial for the defence company, as they are typically more willing to collaborate and grow to scale as a joint effort.
"We've launched our
SME charter
and we're trying to use that to open up doors to get our SMEs together to work in that way and trying to foster that collaboration and help them a bit," explains Ewan.
Ewan Sime, Global Director of Procurement & Supply Chain at Babcock International Group
"So through our supply chain growth team, we've got our partnerships arm in there and the whole point of that team – as well as supporting all of our bid work – is to actually identify our long-term partners and develop their capabilities so that we actually know that for the next 10 years they will be at the core to our business."
The charter maintains practical commitments, proportionate contracts, faster payments, clearer engagement pathways and more support to help SMEs grow. More than that, though, SMEs contribute massively to the UK defence industry, as 99% of UK employers work alongside an SME community.
Resilience can be developed in a multitude of ways, as demonstrated in this panel. Where some companies are moving towards a more localised and personal sourcing model, others are using visibility and technology to manage risk.

title: Congressman presses DOT on Tesla FSD after 43 sleeping-driver videos
content:
Tesla Autopilot
Fred Lambert
| Sep 10 2026 - 8:48 am PT
A US congressman is demanding the Department of Transportation explain what it’s doing about Tesla’s Autopilot and Full Self-Driving after an NBC News investigation surfaced dozens of videos of drivers apparently asleep at the wheel.
Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi gave Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy until September 30 to answer five questions about the systems, which Tesla itself says “require active driver supervision and are not autonomous driving systems.”
What the letter says
Krishnamoorthi, an Illinois Democrat, wrote to Duffy on September 9. He points to an NBC News investigation that identified 43 videos of drivers who appear to be asleep in moving Teslas, 17 of them posted this year alone.
The letter ties that behavior directly to a federal probe that’s already underway. NHTSA’s engineering analysis, EA26002, covers roughly 3.2 million Tesla vehicles equipped with FSD.
Krishnamoorthi also flags a message Tesla vehicles display to drivers: “Drowsiness detected. Stay focused with FSD.” He argues the prompt does the opposite of what safety requires.
“FSD requires continuous human supervision, yet the message appears to encourage use of the system precisely when the vehicle has detected that the driver may be less capable,” he wrote.
Tesla has indeed often posted message on social media about being more rested when driving with FSD.
NHTSA is already one step from a recall
The probe Krishnamoorthi cites isn’t new. NHTSA
upgraded its FSD investigation to an engineering analysis in March
, the final phase before the agency either closes a case or orders a recall. That probe identified nine incidents tied to reduced-visibility conditions, including one fatality and one injury.
The letter zeroes in on a gap Electrek has been
tracking for months
: Tesla’s in-car monitoring doesn’t reliably keep drivers engaged. Owners have found cheap ways around it. Some drape a folded bill over the cabin camera. Others wear sunglasses to defeat the eye-tracking. We’ve documented a whole
genre of drivers filming themselves breaking the law on FSD
and posting it for clout.
That’s the core of the problem. Tesla’s own manuals say continuous supervision is required, and drivers keep proving how easily the supervision check can be faked.
The five questions
Krishnamoorthi wants specifics from NHTSA. He asks whether the agency is aware of the videos and whether they point to a systemic problem, whether it has contacted Tesla about the incidents, and what data it has collected on driver inattention in crashes since January 1, 2024.
He also wants NHTSA’s own assessment of how effective Tesla’s cabin camera actually is, and, pointedly, what findings would trigger a safety recall.
Electrek’s Take
Congressional letters rarely move a federal agency on their own, and this one lands on a DOT that hasn’t shown much appetite for taking on Tesla. So I wouldn’t expect fireworks by September 30.
But the question Krishnamoorthi is asking is the right one. Tesla built the cabin camera as its answer to years of criticism about driver monitoring. And a $20 bill defeats it. If your system detects that a driver is nodding off and its response is “stay focused with FSD” rather than pulling over and forcing hands on the wheel, you’ve designed the monitoring around keeping the feature on, not around keeping the driver awake.
NHTSA already has nine incidents and a fatality in front of it in EA26002, and Tesla has conceded its own software fix would have prevented only three of those crashes. Those sleeping-driver videos just show the behavior Tesla’s design invites. The real question is whether Duffy’s team answers honestly by the deadline, or lets it slide the way this DOT has let most Tesla safety questions slide. We’ll be watching and of course, you can stay on top of our own
ongoing investigation into fatal crashes related to Tesla’s Autopilot and Full Self-Driving systems

is pulling the EX40 from its US lineup, leaving the $60,000 EX60 as the brand’s most affordable EV, at least for now.
Volvo EX40 EV discontinued in the US after 2027
After it
discontinued the EX30
, its smallest, most affordable EV, earlier this year, Volvo is pulling yet another electric vehicle from its US lineup.
The EX40, which initially arrived in 2019 as the Volvo XC40 Recharge, will be dropped following the 2027 model year.
Volvo introduced the updated EX40, which will continue to be sold in Europe, but it will not be available in the US or Canada.
With the EX30, EC40, and now EX40 gone, the EX60 will be Volvo’s most affordable electric vehicle, starting at about $60,000. According to an
Automotive News
report, a new entry-level EV will arrive soon to replace it.
Volvo is reportedly planning to launch a new electric crossover by the end of 2027, starting at under $50,000.
The new EX50 will ride on Volvo’s SPA3 platform, the same one that underpins the EX60, bringing much-needed improvements, including a longer driving range, faster charging, and more interior space.
filed a trademark
with the European Union Intellectual Property Office (EUIPO) under the name EX50 on July 14, 2026. Although the filing didn’t reveal much, it did confirm it will, in fact, be electric.
Volvo EX50 trademark filing (Source: EUIPO)
According to the
report, Volvo’s new electric EX50 crossover will be taller and longer than the current EX40.
While $50,000 isn’t necessarily what most would consider an “entry-level” vehicle, it is still cheaper than the EX60.
2027 Volvo EX60 P6 Plus
starts at $59,795 (including destination fee) and offers an EPA-estimated range of up to 307 miles. The outgoing 2026 EX40 starts at $56,545 and offers up to 296 miles of range.
Volvo EX60 (Source: Volvo)
As the first vehicle based on its SPA3 platform, Volvo calls the EX60 a “game-changing SUV,” offering more than enough range, ultra-fast charging, and improved performance.
Thanks to its 800V electrical architecture, the new EX60 can add 165 miles of range in just 10 minutes.
Volvo EX60 interior (Source: Volvo)
It’s also Volvo’s first EV with a built-in NACS charge port, enabling access to over 29,000 Tesla Superchargers without an adapter.
Measuring 189.1″ in length, 81.4″ in width, and 64.4″ in height, with a wheelbase of 116.9″, the EX60 is about the size of a Tesla Model Y (188.8″ L x 83.8 ” W x 63.4″ H).
Electrek’s Take
While it is sad to see another EV being discontinued in the US, hopefully Volvo comes through and launches the new EX50 in 2027.
The EX40 was a solid electric SUV, and still is. However, with the Trump Administration’s policy changes, including ending the $7,500 federal EV tax credit and the added import tariffs, Volvo has struggled to sell electric vehicles in the US.
Volvo already scaled back on its commitment to go all-electric by 2030. The EX60 is only about $3,000 more than the EX40, but $60,000 is still not cheap.
At about $50,000, the upcoming EX50 will become Volvo’s new entry-level EV, which is still around $15,000 more than the promised $35,000 EX30 that never arrived in the US.

title: Electric car sales doubled in Russia after Ukraine blew up oil refineries
content:
oil and gas
EV sales
Jameson Dow
| Sep 10 2026 - 7:00 am PT
Electric car sales
continue to rise
around the globe, driven to
newer heights
wholly unnecessary oil conflict
. Only a few backwards-thinking countries are resisting the rise… and one of those backwards-thinking countries is now seeing the light, but it’s for a unique reason.
Russia, as one of the world’s foremost oil nations, has never had any difficulty fueling its own vehicles. The abundance of gasoline has always led gas prices to be cheap in the country, which is one reason why electric cars have never taken off there.
Sure, there have been some EV sales, but for the largest and one of the most populous nations on Earth, the numbers have been quite low…until now.
The world is not in a normal time right now. Every country is dealing with spiking oil prices due to the
whims of a senile former reality TV host
, and lots of people are finally coming around to the idea that we should stop using this resource that literally everyone knows we should have stopped using decades ago.
Russia has been somewhat insulated from the effects of the closing of the Strait of Hormuz, primarily because it’s not really connected to global oil markets at the moment, related to
dumb war started by
doddering dictator: that is, Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.
Russia first began its war of aggression by seizing Crimea from Ukraine in 2014. For some reason (read: Europe’s
addiction to Russian fossil gas
), everyone ignored that for 8 years, until Russia decided to invade eastern Ukraine in 2022, starting the current “phase” of the conflict which remains ongoing.
In the last 4 years of back-and-forth in that war, Ukraine has shown significant resilience and has innovated new war tactics, in particular being perhaps the first, or most clear,
demonstration of systematic drone warfare
Most recently, Ukraine has focused on a tactic of penetrating surprisingly deep into Russian airspace and
blowing up oil refineries
Due to Ukraine’s refinery strikes, Russia is finally having difficulty distributing oil, even within its own borders. Reportedly the country’s refining capacity is now only 70% of its domestic usage, with 24 out of the 33 biggest refineries in Russia having been struck.
There are reports of long lines at Russian gas stations, restrictions on fuel sales in several regions, and a ban on exports of gasoline from the country.
All of this has been enough that in the last 3 months of the year, EV sales have
more than doubled
in Russia as compared to the previous year. From June to August of 2026, 26,543 BEVs/PHEVs were sold in Russia, up 118% from 12,187 last year.
This is still a relatively small number – in the same period of time, around 400k total cars were sold in Russia. So we’re talking about a market share on the order of 6% for BEV and PHEV combined, which is still well below the worldwide average (~25% and growing). And, since it started as a small number, a large percentage increase is easier to achieve.
But it nevertheless makes the point that, even in a country that is so heavily committed to oil, electric cars can make inroads when the case becomes so plainly obvious to everyone. Now if only it took less than 24 massive burning refineries to open their eyes…

title: Nanrobot LS7+ review: This 70 mph electric scooter is absolutely insane
content:
electric scooter
Micah Toll
| Sep 10 2026 - 6:01 am PT
There are electric scooters, there are fast electric scooters, and then there are machines like the Nanrobot LS7+ that make you wonder whether we’ve stretched the definition of “scooter” about as far as it can possibly go.
The LS7+ is an absolute monster. It packs a pair of 3,000W motors for 6,000W of nominal power, with Nanrobot claiming up to 10,000W of peak power.
The company advertises a top speed of 74.5 mph (120 km/h), though Nanrobot itself notes that figure was achieved under optimal testing conditions and says typical riding speeds are closer to 58-65 mph (93-105 km/h).
And no, I didn’t take it all the way up to 74.5 mph. I like you guys, but not that much. I also like my skin in all of its current places very much, thank you.
I’m not opposed to going fast, but I choose my risks carefully. I’ve watched the speedometer tick into triple digits on electric motorcycles, but there’s something about hitting those speeds in the same position I ride an escalator that just gives me the heebie-jeebies.
Once I hit the 40s of mph (above 65 km/h) in a standing position on wheels the size of a salad plate, I start to nope out. So don’t expect this to be a top speed review like
on my last Nanrobot testing
, but in every other sense, I was there.
Lots and lots of power
The LS7+’s dual motors provide the kind of acceleration you’d expect from a combined 6,000W setup, which is to say: tons. The thing wants to go like a bat out of hell. And all of that power and torque available at the curl of an index finger means there’s plenty of oomph available for climbing hills too, not just simply rocketing away from a stop.
That’s also why I want to make one thing abundantly clear: This is not a beginner scooter. Not in the slightest.
If your scooter experience consists of cruising around on rental scooters or commuting on a typical 20-25 mph model, the LS7+ is a massive step up. This is the kind of scooter that should be reserved for experienced riders who already understand how powerful scooters handle, how quickly things happen at higher speeds, and how important proper protective gear becomes when you start pushing these performance levels.
Fortunately, Nanrobot has equipped the LS7+ with hardware that at least acknowledges what kind of performance we’re dealing with here.
There’s a steering damper to help maintain stability and reduce the possibility of speed wobbles, which is something I definitely appreciate on a scooter capable of these speeds. You also get adjustable KKE hydraulic suspension and four-piston NUTT hydraulic brakes.
The scooter rides on 11-inch tires, with both street and off-road versions available. The suspension gives it a substantial, planted feel, and overall the scooter feels well-built and appropriately beefy for the performance it offers.
Of course, “beefy” also means heavy. The LS7+ weighs around 119 lb (54 kg), so forget casually tossing this thing over your shoulder and carrying it up three flights of stairs. This is much closer to small electric motorcycle territory than your average last-mile commuter scooter.
Nanrobot also rates the LS7+ for a 30-degree climbing angle and a maximum load of 330 lb (150 kg). I barely approach half that with all my gear on, so I can’t speak for riders on the higher end of that range, but if they build it for climbing huge hills with a lot of weight, then you can imagine how it flew with me on it!
A seriously big battery
Feeding those motors is a 72V and 35Ah Samsung battery, giving us a hefty 2.52 kWh of capacity.
Nanrobot claims up to 81 miles (130 km) of range, though that figure is based on relatively gentle riding at 25 km/h (15.5 mph) with a 75 kg (165 lb) rider. Start regularly tapping into those dual motors at higher speeds and you’re obviously going to get considerably less range.
But that’s exactly why I’m glad to see such a large battery here. High-performance riding consumes energy quickly, and having more than 2.5 kWh onboard means you can actually enjoy the scooter’s performance without watching the battery gauge plummet quite as quickly as it would with a smaller pack.
That big battery is certainly part of what helps float the price all the way
up to $2,299
, though the dual motors, big suspension, and rest of the robust build all add to that figure, too.
Probably more scooter than you need
After riding the Nanrobot LS7+, my biggest takeaway is that it’s actually a pretty good scooter. It feels solid, the suspension is capable, the hydraulic brakes match the performance level much better than mechanical brakes would, the steering damper is a welcome inclusion, and there’s enough battery here to make the ridiculous power somewhat usable.
Sure, I can’t stand the annoying NFC card for unlocking feature, but that’s long been a pet peeve of mine, despite others enjoying the added security benefit.
Suffice it to say though, that in terms of build quality, the scooter checks all the boxes.
But it is also completely, hilariously excessive for most riders.
Most people simply don’t need a scooter capable of somewhere around 60-70+ mph. In fact, depending on where you live, a scooter this powerful and fast may not be street legal at all. Riders should check their local regulations before assuming they can simply blast down public roads at highway speeds.
For riders who have private property or appropriate off-road riding areas, the optional knobby tires could make even more sense. With dual motors, adjustable hydraulic suspension, plenty of ground clearance, and that enormous battery, there’s a compelling argument for treating the LS7+ as an extreme off-road recreational machine rather than trying to shoehorn it into the role of a normal commuter scooter.
That’s ultimately how I’d look at the Nanrobot LS7+. It’s not the scooter I’d recommend to someone looking for their first commuter. It’s not even the scooter I’d recommend to most experienced commuters. Really, it’s for the craziest out there that want something so powerful and fast that it’s barely a scooter anymore.
So if you’ve already ridden powerful scooters, understand exactly what you’re getting into, and want something truly extreme, the LS7+ certainly delivers.
Remember though, that just because a scooter can do 70 mph, it doesn’t mean you have to find out whether you can too.

title: Elon Musk's Boring Company raises $3B at $23B valuation, led by UAE
content:
Elon Musk
The Boring Company
Fred Lambert
| Sep 10 2026 - 5:57 am PT
The Boring Company has closed a $3 billion Series D funding round led by the United Arab Emirates, valuing Elon Musk’s tunneling venture at $23 billion.
That’s roughly four times its 2022 valuation of about $5.7 billion. And most of the case for it sits in tunnels the company hasn’t dug yet.
The company
announced the round
on September 9. Alongside the UAE and its affiliated investment entities, the investor list includes Sequoia Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Temasek, Valor Equity Partners, Vy Capital, Human Capital, Shamal Holding, and Baron Capital. Musk marked the raise with a line about the company’s reason to exist: “Defeating traffic is the ultimate boss battle. Even the most powerful humans in the world cannot defeat traffic.”
The money is earmarked for hiring across engineering, operations, and production, for scaling Loop projects, and for more Prufrock tunnel-boring machine R&D.
The UAE is buying an unproven promise
The centerpiece of the deal is a commitment to build more than 150 kilometers of tunnel across the UAE. That’s on top of the Dubai Loop pilot the company was already awarded: 6.4 km of tunnel and four stations, with construction slated to start late 2026.
So the country leading the round is also the customer for the biggest piece of work it’s funding. Precast production for the Dubai pilot is underway, per the company, but no passenger tunnel is open in the UAE yet.
The one place Boring actually moves people is Las Vegas. Vegas Loop has now carried more than four million passengers, and Clark County has entitled a 123-station network after approving 19 more stations. The company recently started boring its 14th tunnel in the city, its 25th overall.
Vegas has gotten better since we last rode it. When we
took some of the first rides in 2021
, it was human drivers piloting Model Ys at low speed with no Autopilot. Now, it still pretty much that, but there are at least a few more stations.
The main problem with the Vegas Loop is that the company has yet to prove, even in simulation, that it is actually helping with traffic and is more useful than other forms of mass transit.
The company also started its first work in hard rock. Music City Loop in Nashville got its state permit on February 25, 2026, and tunneling began the same day. By August, two Prufrock machines were mining at once, with a third in final assembly in Texas.
A long trail of tunnels that never got dug
Since 2017, Boring has announced roughly a dozen city projects. Vegas is the only one carrying passengers. The rest is a graveyard.
The flagship was the Chicago O’Hare Express, unveiled in 2018 under Mayor Rahm Emanuel: 150-mph pods from downtown to the airport, with Boring footing a ~$1 billion bill. It never had financing or a signed contract, and it was
dead by the time Lori Lightfoot took office
in 2019.
The 2017 Washington-to-Baltimore Loop got conditional permits from Maryland and then quietly
vanished from the company’s own website
. In Ontario, California, a $45 million airport connector ballooned toward $500 million, and Boring withdrew rather than sit through a third-party environmental review. San Antonio’s transit authority picked Boring for a 9-mile airport-to-downtown system in 2022, then said the company simply
stopped answering emails
and the deal died in 2023. Fort Lauderdale’s beach tunnel, selected the same era, has been stuck in the same “ghosted” limbo. Los Angeles lost both the Sepulveda test tunnel and the Dodger Stadium “Dugout Loop” to community opposition and permitting.
That’s the record the new valuation is priced against.
Electrek’s Take
UAE is probably a better investor/project partner for The Boring Company.
They can probably guarantee permitting, and they like to throw things at the wall and see what sticks, which is basically Musk’s and the Boring Company’s way of operating.
My main problem with the Boring Company is that Musk promised me back in 2018 that he would release simulations to show how his loop concept was more efficient than other forms of mass transit, and he never did.
Without that, The Boring Company’s only innovation is boring tunnels a bit cheaper, and even that is up for debate since most of the cost reduction is tied to tunnel size and, therefore, capacity.

10 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Swedish thin-film solar equipment maker Midsummer AB and Indonesian industrial group PT Metalogika Rekayasa Sistem said they have signed a binding investment and industrialization agreement to establish flexible CIGS solar cell and module manufacturing in Indonesia.
Under the deal, Metalogika plans to build a production facility with initial capacity of 20 MW per year, with potential expansion to up to 200 MW annually, to supply solar panels to the Indonesian market and for export.
Midsummer will supply manufacturing equipment and related services for the plant, including its proprietary DUO thin-film production system, and will take a minority equity stake in the new joint venture. The companies did not disclose the exact size of Midsummer’s stake.
The companies said the joint venture will first be formally established, followed by finalization of governance terms, Indonesian regulatory approvals and incentives, project financing, and definitive equipment and technology agreements, before manufacturing equipment is imported.
Midsummer CEO Eric Jaremalm said the company aims to build a long-term industrial partnership in Indonesia, combining Midsummer’s technology and manufacturing experience with Metalogika’s industrial capacity, starting with the 20 MW facility while laying the groundwork for further scale-up.
Firrisky Nurtomo, president director of Metalogika, said the initial plant provides a practical starting point toward substantially larger Indonesian manufacturing capacity with local components, and linked the project to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto’s recently launched program targeting 100 GW of solar capacity nationwide and electrification of 80,000 rural areas.
According to separate company disclosures, Midsummer has previously used a similar model in Colombia, where it is supplying equipment for a CIGS factory with a capacity of at least 100 MW per year, with cumulative machinery orders for that project reported at about SEK 380 million ($39 million).
In a separate announcement earlier this month, Midsummer said it would abandon plans for a 200 MW factory of its own in Sweden, declining an available EU grant, which the company said reflects a strategy focused on equipment sales and minority stakes in partner-led factories rather than self-financed manufacturing.
According to Indonesian government statements and analyst commentary, Indonesia’s 100 GW solar program, launched in August, carries an estimated $73 billion price tag and an ambitious three-year completion target that analysts including the Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR) have described as highly challenging given the country’s current module manufacturing capacity, grid readiness, and financing needs.
Colombia solar module plant
, which Midsummer is developing with Swedish aerospace and defense company Saab, is tied to Saab’s offset commitment following its sale of Gripen fighter jets to the Colombian air force – an industrial-cooperation structure distinct from the commercial joint venture model Midsummer is now applying in Indonesia.
