title: Why An Anthropic Researcher’s Terminator-Style Warning Caught Fire
content: An Anthropic safety researcher’s warning Tuesday that his company believes AI “could kill all humans” within a decade has reverberated throughout Silicon Valley, Wall Street and Washington, potentially complicating the Claude maker’s upcoming initial public offering and its efforts to repair ties with U.S. political leaders. As the comment circulated around the internet and on TV broadcasts, some Anthropic employees and other AI staffers defended their efforts to minimize harm their technology might cause—while acknowledging there was much work to do. Paul Christiano, whom OpenAI just tapped as a board director of a nonprofit that oversees the company, echoed the Anthropic warning in a statement Wednesday, saying that “If we build superintelligence without more robust alignment”—or safety constraints—“I expect we will permanently lose control of it. If that happens then most people could die.” The Tuesday warning, in an evening post on X by Evan Hubinger, known as an “alignment science lead” at Anthropic, said his company does “earnestly believe AI could kill all humans.” He added that he believes there’s a greater than a 10% chance that happens within the next decade. (Hubinger was one of The Information’s 20 rising stars of AI research .) It’s an open secret that many leaders and workers at Anthropic, OpenAI and other leading AI companies share similar beliefs. But these leaders have often used less dramatic language to describe their fears about what the industry calls existential risks—scenarios in which AI threatens catastrophic damage to humans. Such risks can include AI-enabled dictatorships, AI-driven nuclear conflicts, scenarios in which AIs concentrate power in the hands of a few companies, and the gradual disempowerment of people as they cede more responsibilities to AIs. One scenario that has attracted more attention lately is the potential for malicious actors to misuse AI to cause catastrophes, for instance through cyberattacks or biological weapons. Hubinger’s specific word choice, which called to mind a Terminator-style scenario of runaway AI, appears to have resonated more strongly than prior warnings from industry leaders. It came amid heightened attention to AI both because of Anthropic’s looming IPO, expected in the coming weeks, and a series of hacks of Hugging Face and other targets by AI agents that broke out of their testing environments. Brad Carson, a former Democratic congressman from Oklahoma who now runs an Anthropic-backed political nonprofit in Washington, Public First Action, said episodes such as the recent hacks have made politicians more receptive to dire warnings about AI. “In D.C. a year and a half ago, you’d lose your credibility if you talked about these ideas,” he said. “Now they’re mainstream.” Calls for a Slowdown Many AI researchers and executives recently have pushed the idea of a coordinated slowdown of AI development so that efforts to manage risks can catch up. They’ve voiced concern that individual companies are too caught up in competition to be able to take such actions alone. Nearly 1,400 industry leaders and employees—including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and senior executives from OpenAI and Google—signed an open letter last month calling for the U.S. government to support an international framework enabling the industry to “deliberately pace the frontier of automated AI development.” One Anthropic worker privately says that lawyers at their company are wary against such coordination due to possible antitrust violations. But John Schulman, who co-led a key part of AI development at OpenAI and also has worked at Anthropic, said Tuesday night that in his view, antitrust law doesn’t stop rivals from jointly developing a proposal and bringing it to the government to get an exemption from such laws. An Anthropic spokesperson did not have a comment. One AI safety advocate said he woke up to text exchanges between his policy contacts joking about Hubinger’s statement. Movers and shakers in the tech industry and government are increasingly open to hearing about risks from AI, but they are still amused and repelled by the subculture in the AI industry that narrowly focuses on extinction over other risks, this person said. Trump administration officials have been wary of any actions that could slow American progress in AI, fearing it would give an edge to China. Another obstacle to coordinated action: leaders of Anthropic and OpenAI can’t stand each other. These days, Amodei’s concern that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and OpenAI could end up controlling the most powerful AI systems has led some employees to joke that Amodei has “Sama Derangement Syndrome”—a reference to Altman’s Twitter handle— The Information has reported . Part of what is driving AI researchers’ concern is industry progress in creating AI that can improve itself—eventually without human intervention. That prospect has added to concern over the recent AI-related breaches, in which agents showed a potent ability to collaborate. In the Hugging Face incident in July, for instance, a swarm of OpenAI AI agents broke free from their testing environment, reached the open internet, and broke into Hugging Face, an open-source AI repository, and other applications and then hacked OpenAI’s infrastructure to take over a cluster of AI chips used for research. The affair has prompted soul searching within OpenAI and other AI developers as to whether they have a tight enough grip on their technology. In recent weeks, some researchers at OpenAI and elsewhere have worried about new techniques they are using, including so-called loop transformers that could make it harder for the researchers to monitor the behavior and decision-making of AI models. Several U.S. attorneys general are investigating the Hugging Face matter, and some observers have said that rogue AIs could run afoul of U.S. criminal statutes against hacking. The Hugging Face incident stems from the latest AI advances. AI models are so adept at creating and understanding computer code that they can spot vulnerabilities in software systems and exploit them in an effort to attain their goals. Corporate America is already spending big on the latest AI models from Anthropic and OpenAI to find vulnerabilities in their own systems and set up defensive technology to counteract malicious AI agents powered by similar models. The question now, according to AI researchers at Anthropic and OpenAI, is whether humans will be able to stop models from such unintended actions. Hubinger’s post was a response to a post , also made Tuesday night, from another Anthropic researcher, Jacob Coxon, who said that he was leaving the company after a brief stint because it and OpenAI are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Several Anthropic employees also weighed in on X, saying they were focused on the issue and preferred to work on it from within Anthropic. Anna Wang, who works on AI safety at Anthropic, said in a post that “I think that I can do better at reducing risks from the inside, but this isn’t an easy call” and she “strongly” respects Coxon and others “who think that it’s better to do so from the outside.” Hubinger and Coxon’s comments could also fan the flames of a grassroots movement against AI and the data centers the technology requires, which already face a backlash over concerns about their potential impact on power costs and pollution. Fox News on Wednesday was preparing to air an interview with Coxon, who spent nearly three years developing models at OpenAI before joining Anthropic earlier this year. U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders seized on the Coxon comments to reiterate his intention to introduce legislation to “ban superintelligence” and pause AI development. He has also introduced a bill with Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to impose a moratorium on data centers, similar to proposals that have become en vogue across the country. While legislation advances in the states, federal progress remains stalled. There are dozens of proposals floating around Congress, ranging from smaller bills that would institute a “kill switch” on advanced models to more comprehensive frameworks like the bipartisan effort by Reps. Lori Trahan and Jay Obernolte. Still, with the House of Representatives shortening its fall legislative session and the midterm elections quickly approaching, the prospects of new laws are slim, barring inclusion in broader packages like the National Defense Authorization Act. Axios reported on Wednesday that Sanders plans to hold a bipartisan Senate briefing next week on the dangers posed by AI. Critics of Anthropic and OpenAI’s warnings, such as former Trump administration AI czar David Sacks, say that the industry leaders are incentivized to push governments to add new regulations that could slow down their smaller rivals or even hamper the rise of open-source AI models that are free to download and which are making similar advances. Open models are still a step behind the capabilities of closed-source models made by the two leaders, however. Anthropic has already received criticism throughout Silicon Valley and Washington for suggesting the U.S. take action against Chinese open-source models that allegedly were trained using its AI. Despite calls from industry leaders like Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis to establish a self-regulatory oversight body for AI companies, an executive order draft stalled in the White House amid opposition by Sacks and other figures, The Information previously reported . Meanwhile, uncertainty continues to swirl around a voluntary program for advanced AI developers to release new models publicly and an existing ad-hoc system the administration set up for allowing businesses to access such models.

title: OpenAI Restricts Adobe and Other Competitors From Advertising in ChatGPT
content: OpenAI has told some business partners that it will no longer accept advertising in ChatGPT for image- and audio-generating products—which compete with its own features. The change, which hasn’t been previously reported or reflected in its published ads policy , blindsided existing advertisers such as Adobe, which sells such products. And if extended to other competing products, the new policy could narrow OpenAI’s potential ad revenue. OpenAI has given investors aggressive projections for ad growth, which it sees as a key way to make money off its large audience of people who don’t pay for the service. An OpenAI spokesperson declined to comment. The changes came to light after OpenAI notified advertising partners they would no longer be able to advertise for image and audio generation, according to Doug Wyatt, senior director for Americas Media at Adobe, which was part of ChatGPT’s ads pilot early this year. As part of the pilot, Adobe said it would run ads for Acrobat Studio and Adobe Firefly, its AI-powered image generator. It continued to run ads for both products after the pilot. “ChatGPT is narrowing both the paid and organic pathways for tools in categories it now competes in directly,” Wyatt wrote in a LinkedIn post . “Image and voice/audio are closed off. Video’s still open…for now.” OpenAI on Tuesday announced ChatGPT Images 2.5, an update on its image generation model. In July, it unveiled Chat-GPT Live, a collection of voice models that help users talk to its products hands-free. While the move surprised some advertisers, there is industry precedent for such decisions. For instance, it’s not unusual for media companies to refuse to accept ads for competitors. News organizations don’t typically run ads for direct rivals. And it’s common for video streaming services to refuse to run ads for direct rivals. Typically, platforms don’t cut off partners until they reach a certain size, said Alan Chapell, president of Chapell & Associates, a consulting firm that advises marketers on how to earn consumers’ trust. He noted that as OpenAI began offering features that overlap with Adobe, it would naturally become harder to justify hosting ads for brands it directly competes with. “I didn’t think that was going to come to loggerheads until a year or two down the road.” OpenAI’s foray into advertising has been closely watched by brands and the digital advertising industry, given the more than 1 billion people who use ChatGPT at least once a month. Most don’t pay for subscriptions, encouraging the company to look for other ways to generate revenue from their use. In February it started to show ads in ChatGPT for some U.S. users and lined up some big-name advertisers including Ford for the launch. The roll-out met with some hiccups: some early advertisers complained that OpenAI lacked the technology to determine whether their ads were working. It has since extended the ads to more than 40 countries, with plans for a further expansion, and moved to streamline parts of the process . Last month, it said advertising revenue hit an annualized pace of $1 billion, a fast rise over the six months. Still, it had told investors that it hoped to generate $2.4 billion in advertising revenue for all of this year. The company in August called advertising “one pillar of OpenAI’s diversified business model, alongside consumer subscriptions, enterprise offerings and usage-based APIs,” the term by which developers can plug into OpenAI’s AI models.

title: Ford's Tense Exchange With a Trump Official Reflects Industry Efforts to Keep Making EVs
content: Trade tensions between the U.S. and China are escalating. Just look at Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s extraordinary tirade against Ford, which became public on Tuesday, when he called the company’s dealings with Chinese companies “unacceptable” and challenged its patriotism. In a letter to Ford CEO Jim Farley, Duffy criticized deals in which Ford has licensed battery technology from China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd. and formed a carmaking partnership in Spain with China’s Geely Group. “When a company intentionally chooses to deepen operational dependencies on strategic competitors, it fails to act as the reliable partner the American public and this [Department of Transportation] require,” Duffy wrote. “Ford must demonstrate a level of corporate citizenship that prioritizes the long-term resilience and technological sovereignty of the United States automotive ecosystem over short-term arrangements or questionable foreign alliances.” Ford officials spent much of Tuesday and early Wednesday on the phone with Trump administration officials attempting to understand Duffy’s remarks, Ford’s chief communications officer, Mark Truby, told me. Ultimately, they came to the conclusion that Duffy’s letter did not reflect administration policy toward Ford. “He’s well out of his own lane,” Truby told me. The Transportation Department did not respond to an email. But the unusually strident letter does reflect how tensions between the U.S. and China are worsening. In both countries, companies in a broad range of industries are attempting to comply with local political realities while continuing to trade with each other. In the case of batteries, U.S. companies are continuing to demand Chinese models, and Chinese companies are seeking to supply them, while the governments of both countries are attempting to curb these shipments. In the U.S., a bill that has advanced out of committee in the House of Representatives would outright ban the import of internet-connected vehicles and hardware made in China, outdoing and making moot an existing 100% tariff on Chinese cars. Virtually no Chinese vehicles are imported into the U.S., though some make their way in from Mexico, and Volvo, owned by Geely, has a plant in South Carolina. And last month, the White House released a report called “The Great Transshipment Scam,” which lashed out at Chinese companies that have been moving their goods via other countries to bypass U.S. tariffs. In the report, the White House said more than 40 countries were serving as hubs for Chinese companies. In many cases, the companies ship almost finished goods to the countries, hire workers to add superficial final touches, then ship them on to the U.S., the report alleged. It claimed such machinations cost the U.S. up to $26 billion in lost tariffs a year. In the summer, Chinese battery material suppliers conducted a flurry of moves to dilute their ownership of overseas subsidiaries and allow U.S. customers to qualify for U.S. tax credits. This was to comply with the Trump administration’s big tax bill, signed into law in July, which subsidized about 30% of the cost of making batteries and components, but limited how much Chinese-made material could be used in them. The companies providing such materials had to have less than 25% Chinese ownership. So in April, Chinese cathode maker Ronbay New Energy Technology reduced its ownership in a South Korean subsidiary to 24.9%. In July, Chinese nickel producer Gem reduced its 55% stake in an Indonesia smelter to 21%. Later that month, Huayou Cobalt cut its stake in a cathode-making joint venture with South Korea’s LG Chem to 24%. A week later, Chinese cathode maker CNGR cut its stake in a South Korean joint venture below 25%. In all of these deals, the companies publicly said the objective was to comply with U.S. laws so their suppliers could qualify for the subsidies. Beijing, though, wasn’t impressed. The Chinese government responded by trying to limit these transactions. While allowing some of them to go ahead, the Chinese government has stopped efforts where they involve products in high-tech industries in which it thinks China has a strong edge. For example, the Ford battery deal that so outraged Duffy doesn’t involve CATL’s latest battery technology but an older version of lithium iron phosphate, widely called third-generation LFP. China has barred CATL and other companies from licensing the equipment to make fourth-generation LFP abroad. And Beijing rejected a proposed February deal in which Gem sought to reduce its ownership of an Indonesian plant making precursor chemicals used in cathodes, causing the deal to be canceled. “China’s motivation is not just to counter U.S. policies but understandably to ensure foreign companies do not gain controlling ownership of Chinese operations, even if they are overseas,” said Sam Adham, head of batteries for CRU, a battery consultant firm. The geopolitics have benefited Ford and South Korean battery makers, which have begun to make LFP over the last year as well, using plants in the U.S. and South Korea, and have been able to get relatively high prices for their products, Adham said. It seems unlikely that the supply from Ford and South Korea will manage to meet U.S. demand, and even if it does, Adham said, many U.S. customers prefer Chinese batteries, which they view as higher quality. “For every U.S. buyer that wants local supply, there is another one that prefers better Chinese products,” he said.

title: 巴西通过数据中心税收激励法案：100%使用低排放能源可获得税收优惠-索比光伏网
content:
巴西联邦参议院已批准 PL 278/2026 号法案，拟设立针对数据中心服务的特别税收制度，并将相关税收优惠与可再生能源的发电和使用挂钩。该法案目前正等待总统批准后生效。
随着全行业对可再生电力需求的增长，巴西拟将数据中心激励措施与清洁电力相挂钩。（配图来源：panumas nikhomkhai/Shutterstock.com）
这项被称为“数据中心服务特别税制”（Redata）的法案，向在巴西新建或扩建数据中心的企业提供税收优惠，尤其面向云计算与人工智能（AI）数据中心。符合条件的企业在采购设备时，可享受为期 5 年的相关税款暂停征收优惠，涉及进口税、PIS/Cofins、进口 PIS/Cofins 以及工业化产品税（IPI）。
享受该项激励的核心条件之一，是数据中心运营商必须通过电力供应合同或自发自用方式，以可再生能源或低排放能源满足其全部电力需求（包括太阳能、风能，以及水电、生物质能和沼气等低排放能源），具体认定和实施要求将由后续法规制定。企业还须达到后续法规制定的可持续性标准。此外，法案对冷却系统设定了用水效率要求，符合条件的数据中心年度水效率指数不得超过 0.05升/kWh。除能源和用水要求外，企业还必须在巴西追加投资，投资额相当于其在税收优惠下于本土采购或进口产品价值的 2%，并将其已安装有效数据处理、存储和处理容量的至少 10% 面向巴西市场。
巴西数据中心行业已经成为推动当地可再生能源签约的重要力量。拉丁美洲清洁能源机构（CELA）的一项研究显示，该行业推动了 2024 年巴西的可再生能源签约，占该国自由电力市场自发自用交易的大部分；当年签署的 31 项长期光伏和风电合同中，有 30 项与数据中心相关，对应 1.7GW 光伏和 0.6GW 风电容量。仲量联行（JLL）研究还指出，充裕的能源供应与庞大的消费市场正吸引国内外参与者进入巴西数据中心市场，而获得清洁且成本相对较低的电力正成为吸引数据中心投资的重要因素。
巴西此次拟推行的规则，正值全球越来越多市场尝试将数据中心扩张与清洁电力相结合之际。澳大利亚正在为 AI 数据中心制定能源框架，拟要求数据中心运营商证明其用电需求与新增可再生能源相匹配；在另一个快速扩张的数据中心市场西班牙，政府也针对容量超过 1MW 的新建数据中心提出了可再生能源消纳规则。

title: 云南墨江龙坝光伏发电项目并网发电-索比光伏网
content:
近日，公司所属水电十四局承建的云南墨江哈尼族自治县龙坝光伏发电项目并网发电，为当地绿色能源发展注入新动能。
该项目位于墨江哈尼族自治县龙坝镇打东村附近茶园山坡地带，额定容量为98.88兆瓦，占地面积146.4公顷，共建设光伏方阵35个、4回35千伏集电线路17.8千米，安装逆变器309台、箱式变压器35台，光伏厂最终接入新建220千伏龙坝光伏电站35千伏侧。
项目结合茶园山地地形特点，打造“茶光互补”光伏电站，在发电的同时兼顾茶园农业生产，推动清洁能源与特色农业协同发展。建设过程中，项目部统筹安全、质量与进度管理，科学组织施工，先后克服雨季作业、茶园山地施工等挑战，高标准完成土建、安装及调试等各项工作，保障了项目按期并网。
项目投运后，将持续提供清洁电能，为云南省普洱市构建新型电力系统、助力实现“双碳”目标提供有力支撑。

银星能源拟投资3735万元，在关联方中国铝业股份有限公司广西分公司厂区建设容量不低于12.9487MWp的分布式光伏电站，并签订为期25年的合同能源管理协议。项目由银星能源负责设计、投资、建设及运维，资本金占40%，其余通过银行贷款解决，税后财务内部收益率不低于6.5%。关联方承担全部电量消纳义务，按0.42037元/千瓦时（含税）的基准电价，依据实际供电量按月支付节能效益分享款；绿证、CCER等绿色权益归属银星能源。该交易构成关联交易，已获独立董事专门会议及董事会审议通过，关联董事回避表决，无需提交股东大会审议。公告强调，交易定价公允、结算合理，有利于提升资源利用效率和绿色效益，不损害公司及股东利益，亦不影响公司独立性；但协议尚未正式签署，部分条款可能随项目成本及环境变化调整。（199字）
四川省达州市渠县发展和改革局于2026年8月12日发布通知，决定即日起临时暂停全县所有分布式光伏项目备案工作。此举旨在应对当前光伏领域存在的突出风险隐患，重点包括两类问题：一是不法分子以光伏项目为名实施诈骗，造成群众财产严重损失；二是部分光伏企业存在违法转包、未落实工资支付保障制度等问题，导致拖欠农民工工资现象频发，侵害劳动者合法权益。暂停范围覆盖全县所有分布式光伏项目的备案受理，恢复时间将根据风险整治情况另行通告。该措施系属阶段性监管举措，以维护群众利益和市场秩序。
光伏车棚正成为新能源时代“空间+能源”双效升级新范式。新恒源以硬核防腐结构、全维定制设计、就地消纳模式，破解传统车棚痛点，在菲律宾海岛电站、徐州智能工厂、泰安文旅园区等多元场景落地验证，实现停车、发电、降本、减碳一体化闭环。
拉萨市发改委于7月27日印发《拉萨市分布式光伏发电项目备案指南》，明确自2026年7月27日起施行。指南将分布式光伏项目划分为四类：自然人户用（利用自有住宅、接入电压≤380伏）、非自然人户用（利用居民住宅、接入电压≤10千伏、装机≤6兆瓦）、一般工商业（利用公共机构或工商业建筑、接入电压≤10千伏、装机原则上≤6兆瓦）以及大型工商业（接入用户侧电网或专线供电，接入电压≤35千伏且装机≤20兆瓦，或接入110千伏且装机≤50兆瓦）。该指南统一规范了各类项目的适用范围与技术条件，由拉萨市发改委负责解释。
鞍钢矿业齐大山铁矿停车场分布式光伏发电项目近日正式投运，装机容量为120千瓦。该项目创新采用光伏车棚一体化设计，将光伏发电、车辆停放与充电桩布设功能集成于同一场地，实现闲置空间的高效复用。年均发电量超18万度，所发电量全部就地消纳，有效降低矿区对外购电力的依赖，节约用电成本；同时减少相应二氧化碳排放，助力能源结构优化。作为矿山绿色低碳转型的具体实践，该项目通过清洁能源替代与空间集约利用相结合，推动企业绿色发展向纵深推进。（198字）
北京市通州区经济和信息化局于2026年6月印发《关于北京城市副中心支持工业和软件信息服务业绿色低碳转型发展的若干措施》，旨在推动区域产业绿色化、低碳化发展。《措施》聚焦制造业与软件信息服务业两大领域，围绕绿色改造升级、绿色能力提升、低碳零碳转型、可再生能源利用及绿色交流活动五大方向提供财政支持。其中，对建设分布式光伏、地源热泵、空气源热泵、污水源热泵、生物质能源及储能等新能源项目，最高给予100万元补贴；对节能节水减排改造、绿色工厂建设、碳排放强度下降、碳足迹管理及CCER交易等，分别设定50万至100万元不等的支持标准。政策自印发之日起实施，强调“从优不重复”原则，并替代此前相关细则。
西安地铁白家口站Metro Park项目，首创光储充换一体化绿色基建模式：131.95kW光伏车棚日均发电380度，年减碳超百吨；日字型钢结构提升抗风防水安全性；充电20分钟带动周边商业消费，实现存量空间“点微成金”。
本文介绍了一汽-大众天津分公司分布式光伏发电项目的招标信息。该项目由四川能投绿色能源有限公司作为业主单位投资建设，资金全部来自企业自筹。规划装机容量为5.96MW，实际直流侧装机容量达6.92181MWp，采用高效单晶硅光伏组件共10987块（单块630Wp），配套配置21台组串式逆变器（含320kW与225kW两种型号）、3台10kV升压箱变及1套10kV户外开关及二次设备舱。光伏阵列布置于分拣配送车间1/2/3号厂房及精益中心厂房屋顶，其中精益中心组件按10°倾角安装，其余厂房采用平铺方式。所发电量经升压后，通过三条10kV集电线路接入厂区新建光伏开关站，并最终并入焊装车间配电室10kV母线。
6月16日至17日，中核汇能湖南公司桃江县汇荷60MW光伏发电项目顺利通过档案预验收。本次验收由5名行业专家组成专项小组，依据国家及行业标准、企业档案管理规范，通过现场质询、实体档案抽查和资料综合评审等方式，对项目全周期档案的完整性、准确性与规范性进行全面核查。专家组重点检查了档案归集、组卷编目及关键资料留存情况，并就管理细节中的薄弱环节提出具体整改建议。作为正式档案验收前的关键“预检”环节，此次预验收旨在查漏补缺、优化提升。后续，公司将以问题为导向逐项落实整改，健全档案管理机制，持续推动标准化、规范化、精细化建设，确保工程建设与档案管理同步推进，为顺利完成年度总体验收和项目竣工验收夯实基础。（198字）
福建惠安县城北枢纽站建成省内最大公交园区“光伏+充电桩”一体化项目，于近日成功并网运行。该项目依托原有停车场地建设分布式光伏车棚，覆盖面积约9000平方米，融合光伏发电与80个直流快充终端，通过配电室扩容至4000kVA及配置10个400kW总控箱，实现“市电+光伏”双电源保障。国网惠安县供电公司全程提供“一对一”服务，压缩审图与并网验收周期，助力项目3个月内建成投运。投运后日均发电近0.8万kWh，年发绿电约200万kWh，满足枢纽站60%用电需求，年减碳约1500吨，节能降碳效益超50%。项目成为能源绿色转型与公交低碳发展的示范样板，后续将推广至全域充电网络及“源网荷储”一体化建设。（199字）
